prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Do not use colons.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you ask a browser to load shop.example.com/products over HTTPS, a lot happens before the first byte of the response comes back. Knowing the stages helps you read the network panel in developer tools and work out why a page is slow.

**Parsing the address**

The browser first splits the address into parts. The scheme is HTTPS, the host is shop.example.com, the port defaults to 443, and the path is /products. If you typed only a bare word, the browser decides whether it is a site or a search query. It also checks its HSTS list. If the site has previously told the browser to use HTTPS only, the browser upgrades any plain HTTP attempt locally, without sending anything over the network.

**Checking local caches**

Before using the network, the browser looks locally. A service worker registered for the site can intercept the request and answer from its own cache. The HTTP cache may also hold a fresh copy of the page, in which case no request is sent at all. Only when both miss does the browser continue.

**DNS lookup**

Networks route by IP address, not by name, so the browser must translate shop.example.com into an address. It checks its own DNS cache, then the operating system cache and hosts file. If none has an answer, the operating system asks a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public provider. If the resolver has no cached answer, it walks the hierarchy. It asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks those which servers are authoritative for example.com, and then asks the authoritative server for the address of shop.example.com.

The answer carries a time to live, which says how long it may be cached. It often contains several addresses, both IPv4 and IPv6, and browsers commonly race them and keep whichever connects first. Some browsers send DNS queries over HTTPS for privacy, but the logical steps are the same.

**Opening a connection**

With an address in hand, the browser needs a connection. If it already has an idle connection to the same host from an earlier request, it reuses that and skips ahead. Otherwise it opens one. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 that means TCP, which begins with a three-step handshake. The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. This costs one full round trip, and distance matters. A round trip across an ocean takes far longer than one within a city.

HTTP/3 works differently. It runs over QUIC, which uses UDP and folds the transport and encryption handshakes together. Browsers usually learn that a site supports HTTP/3 from an Alt-Svc response header seen on an earlier visit, so a first visit typically uses TCP.

**The TLS handshake**

The S in HTTPS means the traffic is encrypted with TLS, which is negotiated on top of the new connection. The client sends a ClientHello message. It lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, includes a random value and a key share used for key exchange, and names the host it wants through Server Name Indication. That name matters because one server or IP address may host many sites, each with its own certificate. The client also offers ALPN, a list of application protocols such as h2 and http/1.1, so both sides agree on the HTTP version during the handshake itself.

In TLS 1.3 the server replies with its own key share, its certificate chain, a signature proving it holds the private key matching the certificate, and a Finished message. Both sides combine the key shares to derive identical session keys without the key ever crossing the wire. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip, while TLS 1.2 needs two. If the client has connected before, session resumption can shorten the exchange, and 0-RTT can even send request data in the first flight, though with some replay risk.

**Validating the certificate**

While the handshake completes, the browser verifies the certificate. It confirms that the hostname appears in the certificate's subject alternative names and that the dates are valid. It also confirms that the chain of signatures leads to a certificate authority the browser or operating system trusts. It checks revocation status, often through a stapled OCSP response or preloaded lists, and may look for Certificate Transparency proof. If any check fails, you see a full-page warning and the request stops. Common developer mistakes are an expired certificate, a certificate issued for a different hostname, or a server that forgets to send an intermediate certificate.

**Sending the request**

Now the connection is secure, and the browser sends the HTTP request, encrypted inside TLS. It contains the method GET, the path /products, and headers. These include the Host, a User-Agent string, the content types and encodings the browser accepts (so the server can compress the response), language preferences, and any cookies stored for that domain. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the same information travels as compact binary frames rather than text, and many requests can share one connection at once.

**What the server does**

The request rarely goes straight to your application code. It often reaches a CDN edge node or a load balancer first. That layer may terminate TLS, answer from its own cache, or forward the request to an origin server. Behind it, a reverse proxy such as nginx hands the request to an application process. The application matches the path to a route, runs middleware for things like sessions and authentication, queries databases or other services, renders HTML or JSON, and starts writing the response. The server may also answer with a redirect, for example a 301 from the bare domain to the www version, and the browser then repeats much of this process for the new address, reusing whatever it can.

**First byte arrives**

The moment the first byte of the response travels back and the browser receives it, the wait is over. The status line and headers usually arrive first, and the body follows. The time from sending the request to receiving that first byte is called Time To First Byte, or TTFB. Be aware that some tools measure TTFB from the start of navigation, which includes DNS, connection setup, and TLS. Others measure only the wait after the request is sent, so check which definition a tool uses before comparing numbers.

**Where the time goes and what you can do**

A cold first visit pays for DNS, a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, the request round trip, and server processing. Warm visits skip most of that. Several practical habits follow from this.

- Serve from a CDN so the round trips are short.
- Keep connections alive and use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 so they are reused.
- Enable TLS 1.3 and send complete certificate chains.
- Cache aggressively with sensible cache headers.
- Use preconnect and dns-prefetch hints for third-party hosts you know you will need.
- Keep server work fast with database indexes and response caching.

When a page feels slow, open the network panel and look at the timing breakdown for the main document. Each phase described above has its own bar, which tells you whether the delay is in the network, the handshake, or your own server.
